answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1880–1964 · US general; Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area, 1942–45
answer.sourceLine: These exact words appear in Gen. Henry H. “Hap” Arnold’s diary entry for 16 November 1943, where Arnold calls them “MacArthur’s estimate of GB [George Brett].” That makes it a secondhand record, not something MacArthur wrote himself. The idea behind it, sorting officers by brains and energy, was already in print in 1933 and credited to the German general Kurt von Hammerstein-Equord.
answer.confidenceText: Recorded secondhand in a 1943 diary. The idea itself is older.

source.excerpt: Gin rummy score to date - Harry Hopkins 0 - Hap Arnold $3.00 but look out for the deluge. “You can use the brilliant but lazy man as a strategist, a brilliant but energetic man as a Chief of Staff, but God help you with a dumb but energetic man”: MacArthur’s estimate of GB [George Brett] one of the most charming damn fools I have had the pleasure of meeting.
trail: January 1933: the four-type officer typology (clever, industrious, lazy, stupid) appears in Britain’s Army, Navy & Air Force Gazette, credited to Kurt von Hammerstein-Equord. This is the earliest evidence Quote Investigator located ↗.

16 November 1943: at sea in the Atlantic, Hap Arnold enters the compact “brilliant but lazy … dumb but energetic” wording in his diary as “MacArthur’s estimate of GB [George Brett]” (diary text, vol. 2 ↗).
2002: Air University Press publishes the diary in John W. Huston’s edited American Airpower Comes of Age, vol. 2, p. 78. Editorial note 38 identifies Brett (AU Press PDF, archived ↗).
2014: Quote Investigator traces the typology’s many forms and quotes the Arnold diary entry as a “compact instance” of the saying (QI ↗).
source.excerptNote: “[George Brett]” is the editor’s bracket. Note 38 says Brett was relieved “primarily because of MacArthur’s lack of confidence in him” and adds: “It is not clear what prompted this entry unless he had discussed it with Marshall during this trip.”

author.metaLine: 1880–1964 · US general; Army Chief of Staff 1930–35; Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area, 1942–45
author.bio: Douglas MacArthur was Chief of Staff of the US Army from 1930 to 1935. In World War II he was Supreme Commander, Southwest Pacific Area (1942–45), and he later oversaw the occupation of Japan and led the UN Command in Korea. In 1942 the airman Lt. Gen. George Brett served under him as commander of Allied air forces in his theater. In November 1942 Brett was moved to the Caribbean Defense Command, and this quip is recorded as MacArthur’s judgment of him.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The “brains versus energy” grid of officers is one of the most-traveled sayings in military lore. The MacArthur version is just one short, pointed form of it, and the whole idea is credited to at least four other commanders.

items.why: Quote Investigator’s earliest evidence for the four-class typology is January 1933, credited to Hammerstein-Equord, then head of the German army. That is the origin QI favors for the underlying concept (QI ↗).

Huston’s note 38 says Arnold mentioned the adage in his memoir Global Mission without naming Brett, and adds: “The quote is attributed to Frederick the Great” (AU Press PDF ↗). QI also lists a 2011 book with a Frederick version but finds nothing earlier than 1933 (QI ↗).

items.who: Erich von Manstein / Helmuth von Moltke
items.why: QI found the saying credited to Manstein in a 2004 business book and to Moltke on a 2005 website. Both are decades after the 1933 Hammerstein evidence (QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: The popular wording is real 1943 text: Hap Arnold’s diary labels it “MacArthur’s estimate of GB [George Brett]” (diary ↗). It is a secondhand report of MacArthur applying an older officer typology to one subordinate. He did not invent the idea.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The line is a personnel verdict, not a leadership maxim. Lt. Gen. George Brett had led Allied air forces under MacArthur in the Southwest Pacific. In November 1942 he was moved to the US Caribbean Defense Command, where he stayed for the rest of the war (Wikipedia ↗). The diary’s editor says the relief came “primarily because of MacArthur’s lack of confidence in him.”

Arnold wrote the entry at sea in the Atlantic, among notes on gin rummy with Harry Hopkins and a George Marshall anecdote. So it is not a record of a conversation with MacArthur that day. The editor suggests Arnold may have talked it over with Marshall on the trip (note 38 ↗).
context.detailsSummary: How the MacArthur form differs from the 1933 version
detailsBody: The 1933 version credited to Hammerstein-Equord sorts officers into four classes and assigns each a post, with the clever and lazy fit for the highest command. The Arnold diary keeps only three types (strategist, Chief of Staff, and the dangerous “dumb but energetic” man) and aims the last one at a named general.
Quotle.info found no version of this wording in MacArthur’s own speeches or writings. The only documented source is Arnold’s diary.

sourcesVerified.claim: QI quotes the 16 Nov 1943 Arnold diary entry with the exact wording as MacArthur's estimate of George Brett; QI's earliest evidence for the four-type typology is January 1933 (Army, Navy & Air Force Gazette), credited to Hammerstein-Equord; QI lists later credits to Frederick the Great (2011), Manstein (2004) and Moltke (2005 website).

Scanned text of Huston's vol. 2 contains the Tuesday, 16 November 1943 [Atlantic Ocean] entry with the exact quote and 'MacArthur's estimate of GB [George Brett]', plus note 38 on Brett's relief and the Frederick the Great remark.

Air University Press PDF (January 2002, 'Cleared for public release: distribution unlimited') contains the quote on p. 78 and note 38 (pp. 113–14): Brett relieved 'primarily because of MacArthur's lack of confidence in him'; 'It is not clear what prompted this entry unless he had discussed it with Marshall'; 'The quote is attributed to Frederick the Great'; Arnold mentioned the adage in Global Mission, 456.

George Brett commanded Allied air forces in the Southwest Pacific under MacArthur and in November 1942 was appointed commander of the US Caribbean Defense Command, remaining there for the rest of the war.
Wikiquote's Hammerstein-Equord page gives a sourced four-types-of-officer classification (clever, hardworking, stupid, lazy).
